name: ARTEX
origin: Open-source, Go, published on GitHub by "Autumn-27" in July 2026; made unavailable on 2026-10-08, with forks, archived copies and a commercial ARTEX PRO still in circulation
models: External providers (Claude, GPT, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, Kimi); DeepSeek Flash models dominate attacker instances per the FBI
summary: Multi-agent, LLM-driven penetration-testing platform: an operator sets a target and objective, a planner agent chooses steps and worker agents run standard tools, sharing findings. Reported in use by state-aligned and financially motivated actors since August 2026; its own consoles are often exposed to the internet.

name: AntiFox
origin: Open-source fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, maintained under the AntiFox-AI GitHub organisation
summary: Self-hosted, Chinese-language agentic pentest platform whose README calls it secondary development of ARTEX; tied by Arctic Wolf Labs (as read by the Cloud Security Alliance) to IIS and AWS intrusions.

name: PentAGI
summary: Autonomous offensive framework aimed at lowering the barrier for entry-level operators; GTIG observed a customised orchestration platform built on it in the wild.

name: CAIRN
summary: Multi-agent pentest framework built on an observe-orient-decide-act loop in which specialised agents share a blackboard; GTIG has seen it deployed in the wild.

name: CyberStrikeAI
origin: Open-source, Go backend acting as C2 and orchestration server
summary: LLM-native offensive framework presented as a single pane of glass for operations; GTIG has seen threat-actor experimentation with it, not deployment.

name: HexStrike AI
summary: MCP-integrated harness that lets LLM clients drive a large set of pre-installed offensive security tools; GTIG reports experimentation by threat actors and one PRC-nexus intrusion using it with a memory system.

name: Strix
summary: Multi-agent framework for automated vulnerability identification and validation, seen in a PRC-nexus intrusion (GTIG) and in a financially motivated card-skimming operation (Gambit).
